No, thank you, thank you very much and good morning to everybody. So the SOFI report has 2 parts. The first one is the assessment of the numbers of how we are doing in terms of hunger and food security and nutrition. And the second part is a thematic part that contributes to improvement of what is happening in terms of the situation. So today, or yesterday, we launched here in the UN headquarters the State of Food Security and Nutrition of the World 2026, which focuses on a fundamental question, which is, why are healthy diets still too expensive for billions of people? To answer that question, we first need to distinguish 3 concepts that are often confused. Cost, affordability, and consumption. The focus of this office is cost. Affordability is linked to income and income distribution, and consumption, of course, depends on behavioral change. So I could have the money to buy a healthy diet, but if I don't like it, I won't do it. But this report focuses on the cost. So the report shows that the global cost of a healthy diet has increased 25% in just 5 years. reaching $4.28 purchase power parity dollars per person per day. As a result, 2.69 billion people, almost 1 in every 3 people in the world, still cannot afford a healthy diet. Just to give you a reference, the extreme poverty line is $3 PPP per capita per day. So the cost of a healthy diet is above the cost of the level of extreme poverty. One of the report's most important findings is that calories are relatively inexpensive, but nutrition is not. Staple foods provide about half of the calories we need, yet represent only 13% of the cost of a healthy diet. In contrast, fruits and vegetables provide only 5% of the calories, but account for 16% of the cost, so significantly more expensive than cereals, while animal-sourced foods account for almost 30% of the cost. The challenge, therefore, is not to produce enough calories; it is making nutrient-rich foods more affordable, And that's what will reduce the cost of this healthy diet. The report also shows that there is no one size that fits all as a solution. When countries build healthy diets using foods that are locally available and culturally appropriate, costs fall substantially. On average, using local foods reduces the cost of a healthy diet by 34% globally and by almost 80% in Africa compared with a standardized global food basket. This highlights the importance of investing in local production, local value chains and indigenous foods. We also found that where people live matters. In many countries, fruits and vegetables cost more than twice as much in remote areas, rural areas, than in major cities because of the poor roads, the weak logistics, and high post-harvest losses. Perhaps the most important finding that we found is that between 70% and 75% of the cost of a healthy diet is generated after food leaves the farm. So it's not in the farm, it's after it leaves the farm. And the biggest bottlenecks are no longer only on the farm, they are in storage, in transport, processing, cost chains, and wholesale markets. This challenges how we should think about investment. So our analysis shows that investment in rural roads, cold storage, logistics, and efficient value chains for fruits and vegetables generate much larger reduction in the cost of healthy diets than broad, untargeted investments. The report also challenges the conventional policy thinking. Our simulations show that subsidizing staple foods alone can actually increase the relative cost of a healthy diet, so increase rather than reduce. And that's why we are looking for an agenda of repurposing of the support to cereals to move them to more nutrient-dense foods, which will have a bigger return. And this implies that we need to focus on 2 major areas. One is what we call the hardware, and the other one is what we call the software. So the hardware is about the infrastructure that we require to reduce the cost of transportation and logistics, and the software is about the policies. So lowering the cost of healthy diets is one of the most effective ways to improve nutrition and reduce hunger and obesity, which is increasing in the world, and that you will see in the launch of the report on Tuesday, 21st of July in Rome, and we will be open to all of you because what we are seeing is obesity is increasing and we also know through our studies of hidden costs of the agri-food systems, that implies from a total of around $11 trillion of hidden costs, $8 trillion are related to health, which means NCDs, non-communicable diseases, which are linked to the lack of access to a healthy diet. So what we need to do is to focus on 3 priorities: reduce structural costs across the value chain, particularly after the farm gate; repurpose policies and investments towards nutrient-dense foods rather than reinforcing incentives that favor calories over nutrition, and strengthen evidence-based policymaking through better local data, closer coordination across agriculture, health, trade, and social protection. The cost of a healthy diet is not simply another statistic. It is a very important diagnostic that we need to resolve if we want to minimize this enormous amount of hidden costs and enormous amounts of fatalities that come as a result of overweight and obesity. So I thank you. I'm happy to to answer any questions. Thank you.
